strengths: Addresses a practical problem: loss-level token filtering does not translate directly into training speedups because attention propagates gradients to filtered tokens.
Combines structured token compaction with automatic backward-graph rewriting. The Torchgen-based implementation and minimal integration interface constitute useful systems engineering.

Reports meaningful measured efficiency gains across three model architectures: 15–22% lower iteration time at 40% filtering. Timing breakdowns and context-length/filtering-ratio sweeps help characterize performance.
The 15B-token TinyLlama experiment demonstrates improved average downstream accuracy over regular training while reducing target-model training time.
weaknesses: The central claim of sustaining token filtering’s utility advantages is overstated. In Table 2, average accuracy falls from 24.8 for Rho to 20.7 for Collider, a 16.5% relative decrease, with degradation on eight of nine tasks. GSM8K drops from 11.7 to 6.7 and MAWPS from 63.2 to 46.7. Describing this as slight and suggesting hyperparameter tuning will resolve it is unsupported by experiments.

The evaluation does not establish a favorable accuracy–compute tradeoff against Rho. Comparisons use equal training data rather than equal wall-clock budgets or time to matched accuracy. Learning curves, tuned baselines, and quality measurements across filtering ratios are needed to determine whether faster iterations compensate for the substantial quality loss.

Collider changes the gradient estimator rather than merely accelerating the original filtered-loss objective, but its modified backward computation is insufficiently specified. Equation (5) incorrectly multiplies the query/key gradients by sqrt(d) instead of dividing by it. The claimed correspondence between filtering stored softmax activations and compacting Q/K for FlashAttention also requires precise treatment of normalization and saved forward quantities; no numerical equivalence checks against an explicit reference implementation are reported.

Quality evidence is limited to one approximately 1B-parameter model, one mathematical adaptation corpus, and one filtering ratio, without repeated seeds or uncertainty estimates. The other architectures receive timing evaluation only. Claims about large-scale training and communication savings under tensor, sequence, pipeline, or expert parallelism are not experimentally demonstrated.

Comparisons and ablations are insufficient to isolate the contribution. There is no direct experimental comparison with cited token-dropping approaches such as Random-LTD, no simple explicit per-layer compaction baseline, and no study separating gradient pruning from graph-rewriting benefits. A comparison against generic PyTorch sparse GEMM alone does not establish superiority over appropriate structured alternatives.

Reproducibility and cost accounting remain incomplete. Reference-model training and offline scoring are excluded from the reported training costs, limiting comparisons with regular training. Evaluation prompts, decoding settings, reference-data mixture details, and robustness of graph rewriting across execution configurations are insufficiently documented. Reported training duration also conflicts: the abstract gives 4.7 to 3.5 days, whereas Table 2 and the main evaluation give 4.5 to 3.7 days.

strengths: The paper identifies a real systems bottleneck: masking token losses does not preserve gradient sparsity through attention, and generic sparse GEMM may be inefficient at practical filtering ratios.

Collider combines backward activation filtering with dimension-reduced dense GEMM and automated autograd-graph modification. The Torchgen-based implementation and minimal integration interface offer a potentially useful engineering contribution.

The reported performance measurements show meaningful training-time reductions of approximately 15–22% across three model architectures. The timing breakdowns and context-length/filtering-ratio experiments help explain the observed gains.
The 15B-token TinyLlama experiment provides substantive empirical evidence: Collider improves average benchmark accuracy over unfiltered training while reducing target-model training time.
weaknesses: The central quality–efficiency claim is not established against the strongest baseline. In Table 2, average accuracy falls from 24.8 with Rho to 20.7 with Collider, a 16.5% relative reduction, while training time falls from approximately 4.5 to 3.7 days. Collider loses on eight of nine tasks, including GSM8K (11.7 to 6.7) and MAWPS (63.2 to 46.7). Calling this degradation 'slight' understates the results. Matched-time comparisons, learning curves, and time-to-target-quality measurements are needed to establish a useful tradeoff.

Collider changes the training update rather than merely accelerating the original filtered-loss gradient. Removing intermediate gradient paths discards contributions from retained-token losses through filtered context tokens. Sections 4.1 and 6.2 acknowledge this, but attribute the quality loss to hyperparameters without testing that explanation. There are no learning-rate/batch-size studies, gradient-error measurements, or quality ablations across filtering ratios to characterize the approximation.

The modified attention backward pass is insufficiently specified and validated. Equation (5) multiplies the Q/K gradient expressions by sqrt(d), although Equation (4) implies division by sqrt(d) when G_A denotes the gradient with respect to A. More substantially, filtering Q/K before recomputing attention is not automatically equivalent to selecting entries from the original softmax: the original normalization must be preserved. The paper needs explicit equations and numerical checks showing how saved log-sum-exp, outputs, and causal masking produce the intended update in both eager attention and FlashAttention.

Evaluation coverage is narrow for the generality claimed. Model quality is measured only for TinyLlama on mathematical continued training; the other two models receive timing evaluations only. There are no quality results at larger scales or outside mathematics, no repeated-run uncertainty, and no experiments validating the proposed tensor/sequence/pipeline-parallel or MoE communication benefits. Timing on one eight-RTX-3090 configuration does not establish broad systems scalability.

The comparisons do not isolate the contribution adequately. Baselines are limited to regular training and Rho, without a controlled random backward-token mask, a simpler manually implemented compaction baseline, or direct comparisons with cited efficient token-dropping methods. Component-level evidence separating activation filtering, dense compaction, and automated graph rewriting is missing. A benchmark of PyTorch sparse GEMM alone also does not justify broad claims about sparse GEMM implementations generally.

The reported 'end-to-end' savings exclude reference-model training and offline inference, as explicitly assumed in Section 4.3. This is reasonable for measuring incremental acceleration of an existing Rho pipeline, but it does not establish total workflow savings over regular training. Reporting preprocessing costs and their amortization is necessary. The abstract additionally reports 4.7-to-3.5-day training times, inconsistent with the 4.5-to-3.7-day figures in Table 2 and the main text.

Correctness and reproducibility of graph rewriting remain insufficiently supported. Runtime stability and distinctive dimension markers are treated as guarantees, but supported shape transformations, varying numbers of retained tokens per sequence, shape-dependent execution paths, and failure detection are not specified adequately. Numerical validation against an explicit masked-backward reference is absent. Reference-model training details and benchmark evaluation protocols are also too sparse for confident reproduction.

strengths: Addresses a practical limitation of loss-based token filtering: attention makes intermediate gradients dense, preventing substantial computational savings.

Combines structured token compaction with automatic backward-graph rewriting to exploit optimized dense GEMM. The Torchgen-based implementation and minimal integration interface are useful engineering contributions.
Reports meaningful measured efficiency improvements across three model architectures: 15–22% lower iteration time at 40% filtering, with timing breakdowns and context-length/filtering-ratio studies.

The 15B-token TinyLlama experiment demonstrates a useful operating point relative to ordinary training: average benchmark accuracy increases from 17.8 to 20.7 while training duration decreases from approximately 4.5 to 3.7 days.
weaknesses: The quality loss against the directly relevant Rho baseline is substantial, undermining claims of preserving token filtering's utility benefits. Average accuracy falls from 24.8 to 20.7, approximately 16.5% relative; GSM8K falls from 11.7 to 6.7 and MAWPS from 63.2 to 46.7. Calling this decrease slight is misleading, and the suggestion that hyperparameter tuning would recover performance is unsupported.

No matched-wall-clock or matched-quality comparison establishes an improved efficiency–quality frontier. Rho trained for Collider's shorter budget, or Collider trained for Rho's full budget, could materially change the conclusion. Quality is not evaluated across filtering ratios, despite the speedup sweep.

Activation filtering changes the gradient estimator rather than merely accelerating the original filtered-loss objective. The paper lacks a precise complete specification and numerical validation of the modified attention backward pass, particularly how FlashAttention's saved normalization statistics and outputs are handled. Equation (5) also incorrectly multiplies the query/key derivatives by sqrt(d), whereas Equation (4) requires division.

Validation is narrow: quality is measured only for TinyLlama on mathematical domain adaptation, without multiple seeds or uncertainty estimates. Timing covers only 1.1–1.5B models on one eight-RTX-3090 configuration; claimed communication benefits for tensor, sequence, pipeline, and expert parallelism are not experimentally demonstrated.

Comparisons and ablations insufficiently establish the contribution beyond token dropping and structured compaction. There are no empirical comparisons with cited efficient-training methods such as Random-LTD, nor quality ablations separating token-selection quality from the effects of suppressing intermediate gradients.

The reported training savings exclude reference-model training and offline corpus scoring. This is reasonable for incremental comparison with an existing Rho pipeline, but leaves total cost relative to ordinary training unestablished. Reproducibility is also limited by missing detailed reference-model training and benchmark evaluation protocols, while the abstract's 4.7-to-3.5-day result conflicts with the main text's 4.5-to-3.7-day result.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical bottleneck: loss-level token filtering does not preserve gradient sparsity through attention, so fewer supervised tokens do not automatically yield faster training.

Separating query-gradient computation from retained key/value-gradient computation, combined with compact dense GEMMs and automatic backward-graph modification, provides a plausible systems approach to exploiting token sparsity.

The efficiency evaluation spans models from 1.1B to 40B parameters, data and tensor parallelism, and LoRA. Reported end-to-end time reductions of 17.9–34.7% are meaningful, and Table 2 explicitly includes graph-filtering overhead.
weaknesses: The central claim of preserving token-filtering utility is inadequately evaluated. Table 1 compares CENTRIFUGE only against regular fine-tuning and no fine-tuning, omitting the loss-only filtering baseline whose benefits it claims to preserve. Similar training-loss curves in Figure 4 do not establish comparable downstream performance. Downstream results cover only TinyLlama and predominantly mathematical tasks, with no repeated runs or uncertainty estimates.

CENTRIFUGE changes the training gradient rather than merely accelerating evaluation of the filtered-loss gradient. Discarded tokens can still influence retained-token losses through their keys and values; suppressing these gradient paths at every layer introduces an additional approximation. The paper does not adequately characterize this approximation or measure its effect across model sizes, filtering ratios, and training durations.

The attention derivation contains a substantive error as written: Equations (3)–(4) define D as the row sum of the output gradient, whereas the FlashAttention softmax-backward correction requires D_i = sum_j(O_ij * dO_ij). Handling of causal masks across retained and discarded token subsets is also unspecified. Numerical comparisons against an explicit masked-gradient reference are needed to establish implementation correctness.

The efficiency comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the contribution. There are no component ablations quantifying the attention modification versus graph compaction, or comparisons against a straightforward implementation using explicitly gathered activations. The broad claim that sparse GEMM requires over 95% sparsity is supported only by a particular PyTorch benchmark and should not be generalized to sparse implementations overall.

The reported end-to-end savings lack complete cost accounting and a quality-matched comparison. Reference-model training and reference-loss precomputation are not quantified or amortized, although cached reference losses appear in the implementation. Ten timed iterations demonstrate iteration-level acceleration, but not reduced total time to a specified downstream quality.

Reproducibility and generality remain insufficiently established. Appendix C.3 claims an open-source implementation but provides no repository link. Exact training budgets, reference-data mixture proportions, evaluation prompts, and several optimizer and batching details are missing. The graph-rewriting method assumes runtime stability without sufficient validation for activation checkpointing, variable shapes, or dynamic routing; benefits for additional parallelism strategies remain analytical rather than demonstrated.

strengths: Addresses a practical bottleneck: masking token losses does not preserve gradient sparsity through attention, so existing token filtering does not automatically accelerate training.

The separation of query-gradient computation from key/value-gradient computation, combined with compact dense GEMMs and automated backward-graph rewriting, forms a plausible and useful systems contribution.

Table 2 reports substantial measured improvements across several model sizes and training configurations, including data parallelism, tensor parallelism, and LoRA. Reporting graph-update overhead separately is helpful.
weaknesses: The method changes the optimization algorithm, rather than merely accelerating the loss-filtered objective in Equation (1). Dropped tokens can still receive legitimate gradients through their role as context for retained tokens; CENTRIFUGE discards these key/value gradients at every layer. The paper insufficiently characterizes this approximation or establishes when its accumulated effect is acceptable.

The central claim of preserving token-filtering utility is inadequately tested. Table 1 omits the essential loss-only filtering baseline, comparing only against regular fine-tuning and no fine-tuning. Similar training-loss curves in Figure 4 do not establish equivalent downstream performance. Consequently, the reported gains cannot distinguish benefits inherited from the existing selection method from the effects of CENTRIFUGE's gradient approximation.

Utility evaluation is much narrower than the efficiency evaluation: downstream results are reported only for TinyLlama-1.1B on predominantly mathematical tasks. There are no corresponding quality results for the larger models, LoRA configuration, or different filtering ratios, and no repeated-run uncertainty. Speedups across these settings therefore do not establish a reliable quality–efficiency tradeoff.

The backward equations contain a consequential specification error: Section 4.1 defines D as the row sum of the output gradient, whereas the standard attention backward identity requires D_i = sum_j(dO_ij * O_ij). Equations (3)–(4) also leave causal masking and attention scaling implicit. Numerical comparisons against a dense implementation of the intended gradient-masking algorithm are needed to validate the kernel.

Efficiency comparisons and ablations are incomplete. Table 2 lacks a measured loss-only filtering baseline, and there is no breakdown isolating the modified attention computation from graph compaction. The claim that sparse GEMM requires over 95% sparsity is generalized from a PyTorch benchmark without establishing applicability to other sparse implementations. Precomputed reference losses appear in Code 2, but reference-model training and dataset-scoring costs are not quantified, limiting the interpretation of end-to-end savings over regular training.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a system that modifies autograd internals. Appendix C.3 announces an open-source repository but provides no link. Important details such as training duration, reference-data mixture, evaluation prompts and decoding, and handling of causal masks after token compaction are missing. The runtime-stability assumption underlying automatic graph rewriting is also not validated for activation checkpointing, variable shapes, or data-dependent graphs.

Several claims exceed the evidence or are imprecisely reported. Long-context benefits are inferred from experiments reaching only 4K tokens, and benefits for additional parallelism strategies are discussed without measurements. The advertised 26.6% and 9.5% utility improvements are percentage-point differences in Table 1, not relative percentage improvements; MMLU also decreases from 21.7 to 18.7.

strengths: Addresses a practical bottleneck: loss-level token filtering does not preserve gradient sparsity through attention, limiting actual training speedups.

The combination of separately computing attention gradients and compacting token dimensions into dense GEMMs is a sensible systems design. Automatic backward-graph rewriting offers a potentially useful integration mechanism.

Table 2 reports substantial measured savings across models from 1.1B to 40B, including data parallelism, tensor parallelism, and LoRA. Reporting graph-rewriting overhead separately makes the efficiency results more informative.
TinyLlama downstream results show substantial improvements over regular fine-tuning on several mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
weaknesses: The central claim that CENTRIFUGE preserves the utility of existing token filtering is insufficiently supported. Table 1 omits the loss-only filtering baseline, while Figure 4 compares only training loss. Similar training losses do not establish equivalent downstream generalization. Downstream comparisons against loss-only filtering across multiple models and filtering ratios are essential.

The method changes the training gradient rather than merely accelerating the original filtered-loss objective. Tokens with zero direct loss can still contribute to selected tokens through their keys and values; discarding their gradients at every layer removes these learning paths. The paper does not adequately characterize this approximation or establish when its effect on optimization and quality is acceptable.

The attention computation has unresolved correctness and specification issues. Section 4.1 defines D as the row sum of the output gradient, whereas FlashAttention requires the row-wise inner product of the output and its gradient. Equations (3)–(4) also omit causal masking and scaling, and the implementation does not explain how arbitrary token compaction preserves original causal relationships or how the split kernel calls retain the full-forward normalization. These may be documentation omissions, but numerical checks against an explicit masked-gradient reference are needed.

The quality evaluation is narrow relative to the claims: downstream results cover only TinyLlama on predominantly mathematical tasks, whereas larger models receive timing evaluations only. There are no repeated-run uncertainties, quality-versus-filtering-ratio results, or comparisons at matched wall-clock budgets. The reported 26.6% and 9.5% improvements are percentage-point differences, and performance is not uniformly improved: MMLU decreases relative to regular fine-tuning.

The systems evaluation does not isolate the benefits of the attention modification and graph-compaction mechanism through component ablations or compare against a simpler explicit gather/scatter implementation. The claim about sparse GEMM requiring over 95% sparsity is based on a particular PyTorch comparison and should not be generalized to sparse implementations overall. Timing also needs clearer accounting of token selection and reference-loss preprocessing; Appendix C assumes precomputed reference losses.

Reproducibility and generality remain insufficiently established. Appendix C.3 announces a GitHub release but provides no link. Important training-budget, reference-model, evaluation-protocol, and baseline-configuration details are missing. The graph-rewriting correctness argument assumes runtime stability without adequately specifying supported operations or handling of changing shapes, activation checkpointing, and data-dependent execution.
